slides.title: Note 1 · Who
slides.text: Ibn Sina (980–1037), known in Europe as Avicenna, was a physician and philosopher from near Bukhara. By his own account, he had studied most of the sciences of his day by 18.

slides.title: Note 2 · The book
slides.text: The Canon of Medicine, finished around 1025, runs to five books. Translated into Latin in the 1100s, it became a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.

slides.title: Note 3 · Temperament
slides.text: The Canon describes nine temperaments: one perfectly balanced, and eight leaning warm, cool, moist, dry or a mix. Mizaj uses the four main blends.

slides.title: Note 4 · The word
slides.text: The Arabic word is 'mizaj', meaning mixture. It travelled into Persian, Turkish, Urdu and Hindi, where it still means mood and temperament.

slides.title: Note 5 · Not just bodies
slides.text: Classical texts list signs of each temperament that include habits of mind: quick to anger, fond of company, slow to change, deep in thought.

slides.title: Note 6 · Today
slides.text: Unani tradition still uses these ideas as traditional wellness wisdom. Mizaj uses them as a lens for self-reflection, never for diagnosis.
